summary: Defines a basic set of SNMP objects for managing DOCSIS 1.0 cable modems and cable modem termination systems. It was replaced by RFC 4639.

plainLanguage.summary: A control panel for cable internet boxes at home and at the provider's end.

subtitle: Monitoring and managing cable internet devices over SNMP

tldr.problem: Cable modems and the head-end systems controlling them (CMTS) needed a standard way to be monitored and managed remotely over SNMP using consistent data structures.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2669 defines a Management Information Base (MIB) with SNMP objects for both cable modems and Cable Modem Termination Systems, covering software upgrades, provisioning servers, event reporting, and traffic filtering.
tldr.outcome: Network operators gained a standardized way to manage cable internet infrastructure. The RFC was later updated by RFC 4639.

facts.label: Event reporting
facts.value: Via syslog, traps, and local logging

today: RFC 2669 defined the foundational MIB for DOCSIS 1.0 cable modem management. It was later updated by RFC 4639, which extends the MIB with additional capabilities and is the current standard.

sections.title: DOCSIS and Cable Internet
sections.content:
DOCSIS (Data Over Cable Service Interface Specification) is the standard for cable modem systems that deliver internet to homes. Two key devices exist in every DOCSIS network: the Cable Modem (CM), which sits in a customer's home and connects the cable line to the customer's computer or network; and the Cable Modem Termination System (CMTS), which sits at the cable operator's head-end and controls all the modems and routes their data.

Communication flows downstream from the head-end to customers' homes (over shared cable channels) and upstream from homes back to the head-end (using controlled time slots). The CMTS manages the upstream scheduling so that many modems can share the same cable without collisions.

RFC 2669 defines a Management Information Base (MIB), a set of manageable objects and data structures, so that SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) can monitor and control both cable modems and CMTS equipment using a standard vocabulary.
sections.plainLanguage: Cable internet has two kinds of boxes: one in your home (the modem) and a big one at the cable company (the CMTS). This RFC explains how to check on them and fix them remotely using a control protocol.

sections.title: What Is an SNMP MIB?
sections.content:
SNMP is a simple protocol for monitoring and managing networked devices. An SNMP MIB is a tree-structured database describing the values a device can report or be controlled through. Each object in the MIB has a name, a type (like an integer or IP address), and access rules (read-only or read-write).

RFC 2669 organizes the cable device MIB into seven logical groups: the Base group for general system information; the Network Management Access group for SNMP security; the Software group for software upgrades; the Server group for provisioning information; the Event group for logging and alerting; the Filter group for controlling what traffic can pass; and the CPE (Customer Premises Equipment) group for controlling which IP addresses customers' devices may use.
sections.plainLanguage: An SNMP MIB is like a dashboard on a device. Each dial or switch on the dashboard is an object that you can read or turn. This RFC lists all the dials and switches for cable modems.

sections.title: Key Management Functions
sections.content:
The RFC enables several critical management operations. Software upgrades can be triggered remotely: an operator sets the address of a TFTP server, specifies the software filename, and the modem will automatically download and install the upgrade. This allows operators to push new software to every modem without visiting customers' homes.

Server provisioning information shows which servers the modem contacted during boot: the DHCP server that gave it an IP address, the Time server it synchronized with, and the TFTP server that provided configuration files. The boot state object shows whether the modem is operational, waiting for a response, or rejected by the CMTS.

Event reporting and alerting let the modem or CMTS send notifications (called traps) to a network management station when problems occur (for example, signal levels dropping or a device disconnecting). The RFC specifies trap throttling: operators can rate-limit these notifications to avoid flooding the management station with alerts during widespread outages.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB lets operators push new software to modems, see what servers the modem is talking to, and get alerts when something breaks. It also has a volume knob so you don't get too many alerts all at once.

sections.title: Traffic Filtering and Protection
sections.content:
The Filter group defines three types of packet filters. LLC (link-layer) filters allow operators to restrict which network protocols can flow through the modem (for example, allowing only IP but blocking IPX, NetBIOS, or Appletalk).

IP filters work at layer 3, allowing fine-grained control: operators can permit or deny traffic based on source and destination IP addresses, transport protocols (TCP, UDP, ICMP), and port numbers. This supports both inbound filters (limiting what customers can send upstream) and outbound filters (limiting what they can receive downstream).

IP spoofing protection (in the CPE group) prevents a customer's computer from claiming to have someone else's IP address. This is implemented at the point where customer equipment connects to the modem, stopping spoofed traffic at the source.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB lets operators decide what kinds of traffic each modem can send and receive. They can block whole protocols, or just certain IP addresses and ports. They can also stop customers from pretending to be someone else on the internet.

sections.title: Compliance and Status
sections.content:
RFC 2669 specifies MIB objects for DOCSIS 1.0 compliant devices. The RFC required cable modems to implement SNMPv1, the simplest and least secure version of SNMP. Future DOCSIS standards (mentioned in the RFC) were expected to require SNMPv3, which has strong security features.

The RFC notes that at the time, cable modems only processed IPv4 customer traffic. IPv6 support was anticipated for future versions. The design of the MIB reflects these 1999-era constraints.

RFC 2669 was later updated by RFC 4639, which extends the MIB with additional objects for more recent cable modem capabilities.
sections.plainLanguage: This MIB works with old SNMP and IPv4 only, because that's what cable modems had in 1999. Newer versions added more features and stronger security.
